The document titled Summary of Key Information Practical to Countries Experiencing Outbreaks of A(H5N1) and Other Subtypes of Avian Influenza was first published in July 2016 by the World Health Organization (WHO). It is intended to provide guidance to countries dealing with avian influenza outbreaks. 2. This document is an evolving resource and will be updated as new information, recommendations, or publications become available. 6. The document was initially compiled in 2008 to assist WHO representatives in countries affected by outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in animals. It was updated in 2015 following the re-introduction of HPAI viruses in regions that had not experienced outbreaks for several years. 7. Updates in 2015 included revisions to information sheets with input from technical departments, updated web links, and contributions from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). The draft was reviewed by WHO’s Regional Office for Africa (AFRO) to identify gaps and assess its utility. 8. The document provides an overview of key information needed to advise Member States on human health issues related to avian influenza outbreaks in animals. It compiles information from WHO, FAO, other UN agencies, and the World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE). 9. Avian influenza is a highly contagious disease in birds caused by influenza A viruses. These viruses are classified as low or highly pathogenic based on clinical signs and disease severity in infected chickens. Not all infected birds show signs of disease. 10. Outbreaks of avian influenza in poultry can have severe consequences for the agricultural sector, especially if caused by highly pathogenic viruses, which can result in high mortality and the culling of many birds. 11. Avian influenza viruses can infect humans, typically through direct contact with infected birds or contaminated environments. Human infections are rare and are not easily transmitted from person to person. However, there is concern that these viruses could acquire traits allowing human-to-human transmission, potentially leading to a pandemic. 12. Prevention measures in poultry aim to minimize virus circulation and reduce the risk of human infection. These measures should involve collaboration between public health and animal health sectors, following the One Health concept. 13. Surveillance to detect possible human cases should be intensified, and preparation for the first response to human cases in an area should be reviewed. 14. Effective communication is essential during outbreaks. Authorities should provide clear, timely, and transparent information to the public, decision-makers, farmers, and other stakeholders to build trust and enable protective actions. 15. Communication strategies should include mechanisms to monitor public perceptions, address concerns, and ensure that messages are understood as intended. This involves engaging with stakeholders, monitoring media, and integrating findings into official messages and response strategies. 16. The animal health sector is responsible for preventing and controlling disease outbreaks in animals, including avian influenza. Reporting outbreaks in animals is crucial for focusing human health prevention efforts and raising awareness among professionals and the public. 17. The FAO provides technical assistance, capacity building, and laboratory support to countries, promoting collaboration and coordination between regions and stakeholders. 18. The OIE sets international standards for animal health and zoonoses and collects and disseminates official animal disease information. Member States are required to report certain avian influenza infections in poultry to the OIE. 19. National Veterinary Services, typically within the Ministry of Agriculture, implement national avian influenza control measures. Other organizations, including wildlife and international donor organizations, contribute to control and prevention activities. 20. Risk communication strategies should be in place before outbreaks occur and include plans for media communication, social media, community engagement, and partner communications. Consistent and transparent messaging is critical. 21. Measures to reduce human exposure to avian influenza viruses include minimizing contact with potentially infected birds, practicing proper hygiene, and seeking medical help if illness develops. Ministries of Health, in collaboration with other governmental bodies, should develop comprehensive plans to address these risks.
